metadata.title: Complex Cobordism vs Representing Formal Group Laws

nodes.name: Ravenel's question: from formal group laws to complex cobordism
nodes.statement: We attempt to answer a question of D. C. Ravenel's: ``\textit{Infinite loopspace theorists, where are you?}'', or more prosaically: Can one start from the notion of Ring Spectrum Representing [Formal Group Laws] (the functor) and arrive at Complex Cobordism?
nodes.statement_short: Can complex cobordism be recovered starting only from the notion of a ring spectrum representing formal group laws?

nodes.name: Milnor's theorem: $MU$ is Lazard's ring
nodes.statement: Milnor showed that the cohomology ring $MU$ was {\em naturally} isomorphic to Lazard's ring $\Lambda$
nodes.statement_short: Milnor: the cobordism cohomology ring is naturally the Lazard ring.
conclusions: the cohomology ring $MU$ was {\em naturally} isomorphic to Lazard's ring $\Lambda$

nodes.name: Landweber-Novikov: $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ represents Lazard's Hopf algebra
nodes.statement: Landweber \cite{landweber} and Novikov \cite{novikov} show the stronger result that the Hopf algebra $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ {\em naturally} represents Lazard's Hopf algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Landweber and Novikov strengthen Milnor: the whole Hopf algebroid of $MU$ represents Lazard's Hopf algebra.
conclusions: the Hopf algebra $(MU^*MU,MU^*)$ {\em naturally} represents Lazard's Hopf algebra

nodes.name: Notation for $\CP$ and its monoidal powers
nodes.statement: We write $\CP$ for infinite complex projective space, $\CP_k$ for its usual $2k$-skeleta, and will otherwise (try to) emphasize monoidal structures in superscripts: $\CP^{\times k}$ is a $k$-fold direct product, $\CP^{\smsh k}$ a $k$-fold smash, et.c.

nodes.name: Notation: $k!$ as symmetric group, Borel quotient $\bq$, cofiber $/$
nodes.statement: We use $k!$ as the name of the symmetric group on $[k]$ (the von Neumann ordinal, for definiteness), whose cardinality is the usual significance of ``$k!$''; Borel quotient is denoted $\bq $ and cofiber is $/$; in particular $*\bq G \simeq \deloop G$.
differentia: Borel quotient is denoted $\bq $ and cofiber is $/$

nodes.name: Generalized Thom space (twisted half-smash) $\Th(X,F)$
nodes.statement: In any case, our twisted half smashes, or generalized Thom spaces, are denoted and defined as $$ \Th(X,F) \simeq E/X $$ where $X \to E \to X$ is a section/retract with fibers $F\to E \to X$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Th(X,F)$ is the cofiber $E/X$ of a section/retract $X\to E\to X$ with fiber $F$.
nodes.definiendum: twisted half smashes, or generalized Thom spaces
differentia: where $X \to E \to X$ is a section/retract with fibers $F\to E \to X$

nodes.name: Thom space of a group action as a cofiber of Borel quotients
nodes.statement: In particular, the Thom space of a group action in the pointed category is a cofiber of Borel quotients: $$ \Th(\deloop G, X) \simeq (X\bq G) / (*\bq G) .$$
nodes.statement_short: For a group action, $\Th(\deloop G,X)$ is the cofiber of $*\bq G \to X\bq G$.
nodes.definiendum: the Thom space of a group action in the pointed category

nodes.name: Radically homotopical, model-category-free perspective
nodes.statement: We make frequent use of geometric arguments to study classifying spaces of {\em geometric things} and sometimes use well-known skeleta; nonetheless our perspective is {\em radically} homotopical: we do not work in any particular model categories (in particular, we never use notions of fibration or cofibration, nor mention weakness of equivalences), but in a setting where ``commuting diagrams'' come with (usually unnamed, but as-specific-as-sensible) homotopies, of whatever shape is required. In the metalanguage around Homtopy Type Theory, ``commutativity is data''. In fact what diagrams we use are, almost exclusively, coherent cubes, which are diagrams all of whose cubical facets are ``contractible'', to the extent that makes sense; and whenever we say ``colimit'' or ``cofiber'' or ``fiber'' we mean, exclusively, {\em homotopy}-colimit, {\em homotopy}-(co)fiber, et.c.
nodes.statement_short: Methodological stance: no model categories; commuting diagrams carry homotopy data, and all limits/colimits are homotopy ones.

nodes.name: Distributivity (the result of Mather's Cube theorems)
nodes.statement: Lastly, within the usual Kelley category of CG[w]Hf spaces, one has Mather's Cube theorems; we call the {\em result} of Mather's theorems (and its finitary corollaries over any colimit) {\em distributivity}, after the obvious arithmetic analogue.
nodes.statement_short: The conclusion of Mather's Cube theorems, plus its finitary corollaries over colimits, is named `distributivity'.
differentia: (and its finitary corollaries over any colimit)

nodes.name: Finitary distributivity taken as an axiom of unstable homotopy
nodes.statement: and we use finitary distributivity as a general {\em axiom} of [unstable] homotopy.

nodes.name: A complex oriented commutative ring spectrum supports a formal group law
nodes.statement: The place we start is: a Complex Oriented Commutative Ring Spectrum probably supports a Formal Group Law. That is, given a ring spectrum $\Lambda$ (suitable for Atiyah-Hirzebruch purposes) and a class $g : \Lambda^2(\CP)$ extending the fundamental class $\eta: \Lambda^2(\sph^2)\sim \Lambda^0(*)\ni 1$, pull-back along tensor product of lines $\otimes: \CP\times\CP \to \CP$ induces a ring homomorphism $\Lambda^*(\CP) \to \Lambda^*(\CP\times\CP)$ which (due to the goodness of $g$ and collapsing spectral sequences) gives a formal group law $$ \Lambda^*(\sph)[x] \to \Lambda^*(\sph)[x\otimes 1,1\otimes x] .$$
nodes.statement_short: An orientation class $g\in\Lambda^2(\CP)$ pulled back along $\otimes:\CP\times\CP\to\CP$ yields a formal group law over $\Lambda^*(\sph)$.
assumptions: given a ring spectrum $\Lambda$ (suitable for Atiyah-Hirzebruch purposes) and a class $g : \Lambda^2(\CP)$ extending the fundamental class $\eta: \Lambda^2(\sph^2)\sim \Lambda^0(*)\ni 1$
conclusions: a Complex Oriented Commutative Ring Spectrum probably supports a Formal Group Law
gives a formal group law $$ \Lambda^*(\sph)[x] \to \Lambda^*(\sph)[x\otimes 1,1\otimes x] .$$

nodes.name: The principal tools: collapsing Atiyah-Hirzebruch sequences and $H^*(\CP)=\ZZ[x]$
nodes.statement: It may be worth remarking that the principal tools in the preceding are: the Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence collapses for an even-concentrated cohomology theory over an even-concentrated space; and the ordinary cohomology of $\CP$ is the ordinary polynomial ring $\ZZ[x]$; this feature it shares with the \textit{homology} of the odd-sphere loopspaces $\Omega \sph^{2n+1}$; indeed the Hopf Algebras $H^*(\CP)$ and $H_*(\Omega\sph^{2n+1})$ are isomorphic, which means it's hard to see (except that $\otimes$ is plainly special) why one should prefer {\em co}homology for FGL purposes.
nodes.statement_short: The argument only used AHSS collapse in even degrees and $H^*(\CP)=\ZZ[x]$ — a property shared by $H_*(\Omega\sph^{2n+1})$, so cohomology is not obviously preferred.

nodes.name: What is the minimal complex-oriented ring spectrum?
nodes.statement: {\em Having} chosen to reflect FGLs by complex-oriented ring spectra, one can clearly ask: what is the minimal complex-oriented ring spectrum? And this in turn means: what is the ring spectrum $\Lambda$ {\em generated by} a map $\CP \to \Lambda_2$?
nodes.statement_short: Find the ring spectrum $\Lambda$ freely generated by a map $\CP\to\Lambda_2$.

nodes.name: Model of ring spectra: $E_\infty$ algebras in $E_\infty$ spaces with spectral smash
nodes.statement: Answering such a question will proceed most simply if we choose a particular model (not to say ``model category''!) of ring spectra; and for this we choose the simplest available option, algebras of the $E_\infty$ operad in the homotopical monoidal category: ($E_\infty$ spaces, spectral smash product).

nodes.name: The approximating spaces $L_{2k} = \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k})$
nodes.statement: Using this model (cf. \cite{mayRings}) it is straightforward that our ring spectrum $\Lambda$ should be approximated by the spaces $$ L_{2k} = \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) $$ with prespectrum maps induced by $$ \sph^2 \smsh L_{2k} \to \CP \smsh L_{2k} \to L_{2k+2} $$
nodes.statement_short: $L_{2k}$ is the generalized Thom space of the $k!$-action on $\CP^{\smsh k}$, with the evident prespectrum structure maps.
differentia: with prespectrum maps induced by $$ \sph^2 \smsh L_{2k} \to \CP \smsh L_{2k} \to L_{2k+2} $$

nodes.name: Warning: no reason for $L_{2k}$ to be evenly concentrated
nodes.statement: The remainder of this note is directed towards studying these $L_{2k}$ to show that they do in fact approximate, in the rough, {\em something}, and in the fine, compare it to our beloved $MU$; but, note: it is already looking difficult, in that there seems little reason for $L_{2k}$ to be homologically concentrated in even degree!
nodes.statement_short: The programme is to compare $L_{2k}$ with $MU$, but even-degree concentration — the usual crutch — is not available.

nodes.name: The $L_{2k}$ are already universal
nodes.statement: But the reason is simple: the $L_{2k}$ are already universal.
conclusions: the $L_{2k}$ are already universal

nodes.name: Argument that the single-operation approximants $L_{2k}$ suffice
nodes.statement: More: it is required, for any commutative ring spectrum $E$ and orientation $\CP\to E_2$, that we have {\em ring maps} $\Lambda_k \to E_k$; and ``ring maps'' {\em means} commutativity $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \Th(\deloop k!, \Lambda_l^{\smsh k}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \Th(\deloop k!,E_l^{\smsh k}) \ar[d]\\ \Lambda_{kl} \ar[r] & E_{kl} }\end{xy} $$ Thus on the one hand, it is {\em necessary} that $$\begin{xy} \xymatrix{ \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \Th(\deloop k!, E_2^{\smsh k}) \ar[d] \\ L_{2k} \ar[r] & E_{2k} } \end{xy} $$ commutes; and on the other hand, there is {\em exactly} one way for this to happen when the left arrow is an identity.
nodes.statement_short: Unwind what a ring map out of the approximants must be: the required square is forced, and is uniquely fillable once the left arrow is an identity.

nodes.name: Ring maps into $E$ mean commutativity of the Thom-space square
nodes.statement: More: it is required, for any commutative ring spectrum $E$ and orientation $\CP\to E_2$, that we have {\em ring maps} $\Lambda_k \to E_k$; and ``ring maps'' {\em means} commutativity $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \Th(\deloop k!, \Lambda_l^{\smsh k}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \Th(\deloop k!,E_l^{\smsh k}) \ar[d]\\ \Lambda_{kl} \ar[r] & E_{kl} }\end{xy} $$
nodes.statement_short: Spell out that a ring map to $E$ is exactly commutativity of the square of Thom spaces.

nodes.name: Necessity and uniqueness when the left arrow is an identity
nodes.statement: Thus on the one hand, it is {\em necessary} that $$\begin{xy} \xymatrix{ \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \Th(\deloop k!, E_2^{\smsh k}) \ar[d] \\ L_{2k} \ar[r] & E_{2k} } \end{xy} $$ commutes; and on the other hand, there is {\em exactly} one way for this to happen when the left arrow is an identity.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude: the square is necessary, and admits exactly one filling, so the approximants are universal.

nodes.name: Direct sum map $\bigoplus : \CP^{\times k} \bq k! \to \deloop U(k)$
nodes.statement: Since direct sum is plainly a useful $E_\infty$ construction on complex vector spaces (this is, after Segal, what makes $\deloop U$ an infinite loopspace), it is the most natural thing in geometry to consider the maps $$ \bigoplus : \CP^{\times k} \bq k! \to \deloop U(k).$$
nodes.statement_short: Direct sum of lines gives an $E_\infty$ map from the symmetrized product of projective spaces to $\deloop U(k)$.

nodes.name: Identification of $MU(k)$ as the cofiber of $\deloop U(k-1)\to\deloop U(k)$
nodes.statement: We connect the Thom space $\Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k})$ via this natural construction to the classic cobordism spectrum $MU$ using a fact, which surely is well-known but not often mentioned: the ordinary Thom spaces $MU(k)$ are the cofibers of the usual maps $\deloop U(k-1)\to \deloop U(k)$. That is: the Thom space is described as the quotient (cofiber) of a (vector space or disk) bundle by the inclusion of the bundle of spheres (at-infinity or unit spheres); but for homotopy purposes, the important feature is the bundle of spheres itself, which is to say the map $$ E \to \deloop U(k) $$ whose fibers are the unit spheres of the tautological bundle. The usual discussion of disk bundle and sphere-at-infinity acheives the necessary trivial-fibration$\circ$cofibration replacement in any of the classic model-category structures; however, the result of the construction is the (we now don't need to {\em say} ``homotopy'') cofiber. Therefore, for the purposes of homotopy, it is sufficient to identify the type of the map $E\to U(k)$; but this is easy: the unit sphere is the (Borel, or ordinary) quotient $U(k)\bq U(k-1)$; the canonical action of $U(k)$ on this has Borel quotient equivalent to $\deloop U(k-1)$ and by functoriality of $\deloop$ the quotient {\em map} is the fiber map $$ \sph^{2k-1} \to \deloop U(k-1) \to \deloop U(k) $$
nodes.statement_short: Replace the disk/sphere-bundle description of the Thom space by its homotopy cofiber, then identify the sphere bundle as $\deloop U(k-1)\to\deloop U(k)$.

nodes.name: The Thom space as quotient by the bundle of spheres
nodes.statement: That is: the Thom space is described as the quotient (cofiber) of a (vector space or disk) bundle by the inclusion of the bundle of spheres (at-infinity or unit spheres); but for homotopy purposes, the important feature is the bundle of spheres itself, which is to say the map $$ E \to \deloop U(k) $$ whose fibers are the unit spheres of the tautological bundle.
nodes.statement_short: Set up: what matters homotopically is the unit-sphere bundle $E \to \deloop U(k)$.

nodes.name: Disk/sphere-at-infinity replacement computes the homotopy cofiber
nodes.statement: The usual discussion of disk bundle and sphere-at-infinity acheives the necessary trivial-fibration$\circ$cofibration replacement in any of the classic model-category structures; however, the result of the construction is the (we now don't need to {\em say} ``homotopy'') cofiber.
nodes.statement_short: Observe that the classical model-category replacement just produces the homotopy cofiber.

nodes.name: Identify the sphere bundle as $\deloop U(k-1)\to \deloop U(k)$
nodes.statement: Therefore, for the purposes of homotopy, it is sufficient to identify the type of the map $E\to U(k)$; but this is easy: the unit sphere is the (Borel, or ordinary) quotient $U(k)\bq U(k-1)$; the canonical action of $U(k)$ on this has Borel quotient equivalent to $\deloop U(k-1)$ and by functoriality of $\deloop$ the quotient {\em map} is the fiber map $$ \sph^{2k-1} \to \deloop U(k-1) \to \deloop U(k) $$
nodes.statement_short: Conclude via $U(k)\bq U(k-1)\simeq\sph^{2k-1}$ that the sphere bundle is $\deloop U(k-1)\to\deloop U(k)$.

nodes.name: $MU(k) \simeq \deloop U(k) / \deloop U(k-1)$
nodes.statement: $$ MU(k) \simeq \deloop U(k) / \deloop U(k-1) $$
conclusions: $$ MU(k) \simeq \deloop U(k) / \deloop U(k-1) $$

nodes.name: Pasting diagram of pushouts presenting $\Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k})$
nodes.statement: There is a pasting diagram of pushouts $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k \CP \bq k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \CP^{\times k}\bq k! \ar[d] \\ \deloop k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \CP^{\smsh k}\bq k! \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r] & \Th(\deloop k!, \CP^{\smsh k}) } \end{xy} $$
nodes.statement_short: $\Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k})$ is built by pasting two pushouts starting from the fat wedge $W^k\CP\bq k!$.
conclusions: There is a pasting diagram of pushouts $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k \CP \bq k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \CP^{\times k}\bq k! \ar[d] \\ \deloop k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \CP^{\smsh k}\bq k! \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r] & \Th(\deloop k!, \CP^{\smsh k}) } \end{xy} $$

nodes.name: Cube of coordinate planes
nodes.statement: In any category with products, for any pointed object $* \to X$ and any $k:\NN$ there is a commuting $k$-cube of coordinate planes: the cube of pullbacks of $k$ inclusions $$ X^{k-1} \to X^k $$ which themselves are the fibers {\em at} $*\to X$ of the $k$ defining structure maps $X^k \to X$.
nodes.statement_short: For a pointed object $X$, the $k$-cube whose vertices are pullbacks of the inclusions $X^{k-1}\to X^k$.
nodes.genus: the cube of pullbacks of $k$ inclusions
differentia: which themselves are the fibers {\em at} $*\to X$ of the $k$ defining structure maps $X^k \to X$

nodes.name: Blooms and the fat wedge $W^k X$
nodes.statement: Though it is more generality than we need, different truncations of these diagrams (\dots the truncations should have a snappy name; I will call them ``blooms'') have colimits that generalize wedge sums, including, in particular, the ``fat wedge''; for the sake of convenience in notating $W^k X \bq k!$, we have chosen to index the fat wedges by the dimension of ambient cube defining them, rather than the degree of their petals.
nodes.statement_short: Truncations (`blooms') of the coordinate-plane cube have colimits generalizing wedges; the fat wedge $W^kX$ is indexed by the ambient cube dimension.
differentia: have colimits that generalize wedge sums, including, in particular, the ``fat wedge''
we have chosen to index the fat wedges by the dimension of ambient cube defining them, rather than the degree of their petals

nodes.name: Construction of the equivariant lifting cube
nodes.statement: There isn't much choice about the maps towards the terminal vertex in the wanted diagram: we have direct sum, $\CP^{k-1}\to \deloop U(k-1)$, and anything hugely different is likely to be too forgetful. We have already described the map $\deloop U(k-1)\to \deloop U(k)$ as the tautological sphere bundle over $\deloop U(k)$ $$ \sph^{2k-1} \to \deloop U(k-1) \to \deloop U(k) $$ which is to say that a point of $\deloop U(k-1)$ over $V:\deloop U(k)$ corresponds to {\em a unit vector in $V$}, which also articulates the sense in which the map $\deloop U(k-1)\to \deloop U(k)$ is direct sum {\em with $\CC$} and not just {\em any line}; in terms of the space $\deloop U(k-1)$ as classifier of $k-1$-dimensional complex vector spaces, a unit vector in $V$ corresponds to {\em the orthogonal complement} of that vector; and so a composite $\deloop U(k-2) \to \deloop U(k)$ further corresponds to {\em an ordered pair} of orthogonal unit vectors in $V$, and classifies the orthogonal complement of their span, et.c. What matters for us is: the action of $k!$ on the relevant cubes {\em permutes these orders}; or, for now passing over the action of $k!$, the possible obstruction to homotopy commutativity in $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \CP^{\times k-2} \ar[r] \ar[d] & \CP^{\times k-1} \ar[d] \\ \CP^{\times k-1} \ar[r] & \deloop U(k-1) }\end{xy}$$ is that the two routes have chosen orthogonal vectors in $V$, the unambiguous vector space specified by the unambiguous composite $\CP^{\times k-2} \to \CP^{\times k} \to \deloop U(k)$. To specify the commutativity of the square, it is sufficient to specify a homotopy in unit vectors between these orthogonal two. Happily, a basis for a complex space induces an inclusion of a real space with a basis, and in a real space with a basis, the positive orthant of the unit sphere does everything we need! Being described in such dimension-agnostic terms, it is also clear how to generalize the argument to other layers of the cube, and commutativity with the already-known maps to $\deloop U(k)$. And, hopefully, the equivariance of the construction is also sufficiently evident.
nodes.statement_short: Build the coherent cube by hand: the obstruction to commutativity is a choice of orthogonal unit vectors, contracted using the positive orthant of a real unit sphere.

nodes.name: The terminal-vertex maps are forced to be direct sum
nodes.statement: There isn't much choice about the maps towards the terminal vertex in the wanted diagram: we have direct sum, $\CP^{k-1}\to \deloop U(k-1)$, and anything hugely different is likely to be too forgetful.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the maps towards the terminal vertex as direct sum.

nodes.name: Points of $\deloop U(k-1)$ over $\deloop U(k)$ as unit vectors
nodes.statement: We have already described the map $\deloop U(k-1)\to \deloop U(k)$ as the tautological sphere bundle over $\deloop U(k)$ $$ \sph^{2k-1} \to \deloop U(k-1) \to \deloop U(k) $$ which is to say that a point of $\deloop U(k-1)$ over $V:\deloop U(k)$ corresponds to {\em a unit vector in $V$}, which also articulates the sense in which the map $\deloop U(k-1)\to \deloop U(k)$ is direct sum {\em with $\CC$} and not just {\em any line}; in terms of the space $\deloop U(k-1)$ as classifier of $k-1$-dimensional complex vector spaces, a unit vector in $V$ corresponds to {\em the orthogonal complement} of that vector; and so a composite $\deloop U(k-2) \to \deloop U(k)$ further corresponds to {\em an ordered pair} of orthogonal unit vectors in $V$, and classifies the orthogonal complement of their span, et.c.
nodes.statement_short: Reinterpret the tower $\deloop U(k-j)\to\deloop U(k)$ as ordered tuples of orthogonal unit vectors.

nodes.name: The obstruction to commutativity is a pair of orthogonal vectors
nodes.statement: What matters for us is: the action of $k!$ on the relevant cubes {\em permutes these orders}; or, for now passing over the action of $k!$, the possible obstruction to homotopy commutativity in $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ \CP^{\times k-2} \ar[r] \ar[d] & \CP^{\times k-1} \ar[d] \\ \CP^{\times k-1} \ar[r] & \deloop U(k-1) }\end{xy}$$ is that the two routes have chosen orthogonal vectors in $V$, the unambiguous vector space specified by the unambiguous composite $\CP^{\times k-2} \to \CP^{\times k} \to \deloop U(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Isolate the obstruction: the two routes around the square pick different orthogonal unit vectors.

nodes.name: Contract the obstruction in the positive orthant and generalize
nodes.statement: To specify the commutativity of the square, it is sufficient to specify a homotopy in unit vectors between these orthogonal two. Happily, a basis for a complex space induces an inclusion of a real space with a basis, and in a real space with a basis, the positive orthant of the unit sphere does everything we need! Being described in such dimension-agnostic terms, it is also clear how to generalize the argument to other layers of the cube, and commutativity with the already-known maps to $\deloop U(k)$. And, hopefully, the equivariance of the construction is also sufficiently evident.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude: the positive orthant of the real unit sphere supplies the homotopy, and the construction is dimension-agnostic and equivariant.

nodes.name: Lifting square and the comparison map $\Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) \to MU(k)$
nodes.statement: We therefore claim a commutative square $$ \xymatrix{W^k\CP \bq k! \ar[r]\ar[d] & \deloop U(k-1)\ar[d] \\ \CP^{\times k} \bq k! \ar[r] & \deloop U(k)} $$ and hence a map $$ \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) \to MU(k) .$$
nodes.statement_short: A commutative square lifting $W^k\CP\bq k!\to\deloop U(k-1)$, hence a map from the Thom space to $MU(k)$.
conclusions: a commutative square $$ \xymatrix{W^k\CP \bq k! \ar[r]\ar[d] & \deloop U(k-1)\ar[d] \\ \CP^{\times k} \bq k! \ar[r] & \deloop U(k)} $$
a map $$ \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) \to MU(k) .$$

nodes.name: Fiber sequence $\sph^{2k-1} \to W^k\CP \bq k! \to \CP^{\times k} \bq k!$
nodes.statement: The fiber of including a fat wedge in a product $W^k X \to X^k$, (and therefore the fiber of the map $W^k \CP \bq k! \to \CP^{\times k} \bq k!$ as well) is, by Distributivity, the $k$-fold self-join of the loopspace $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$; and so we have the small surprise: a fiber sequence $$ \sph^{2k-1} \to W^k\CP \bq k! \to \CP^{\times k} \bq k! $$
nodes.statement_short: By distributivity the fiber of $W^kX\to X^k$ is the $k$-fold join $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$, giving a $\sph^{2k-1}$ fiber sequence for $\CP$.
assumptions: The fiber of including a fat wedge in a product $W^k X \to X^k$, (and therefore the fiber of the map $W^k \CP \bq k! \to \CP^{\times k} \bq k!$ as well)
conclusions: is, by Distributivity, the $k$-fold self-join of the loopspace $(\Omega X)^{\star k}$
a fiber sequence $$ \sph^{2k-1} \to W^k\CP \bq k! \to \CP^{\times k} \bq k! $$

nodes.name: The lifting square is a pullback
nodes.statement: In fact, we will argue that the square we already constructed by an interpolation argument (resulting in Lemma \ref{liftingsquare}), is a pullback.
nodes.statement_short: The square of Lemma \ref{liftingsquare} is a pullback, i.e. $R_k \simeq W^k\CP$.
conclusions: the square we already constructed by an interpolation argument (resulting in Lemma \ref{liftingsquare}), is a pullback

nodes.name: Fiberwise join decomposition identifying $R_k \simeq W^k \CP$
nodes.statement: We will work on the $k!$-space rather than the borel quotient, for now, but the equivariance of the argument should be clear. To keep a handle on things, we'll start by naming the pullback itself $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \deloop U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ \CP^{\times k} \ar[r]_\oplus & \deloop U(k) }\end{xy} $$ To begin with, note once more that a point of $R_k$ over $x : \CP^{\times k} $ is specified by a unit vector {\em in} $\oplus x$. Note furthermore that $x$ {\em is} (or might as well be) a {\em split} complex vector space: it comes with a prefered list of independent lines; this in turn gives the unit sphere in $\oplus x$, {\em canonically}, the structure of a join of (unpointed) circles: $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ {\underset{j}{\bigstar}\,\sph(x_j)} \ar[r] \ar[d] & R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \deloop U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r]_{(x_j|j=1\dots k)} & \CP^{\times k} \ar[r] & \deloop U(k) }\end{xy}$$ Moreover, this join itself is the colimit of the penultimate bloom within the product cube of the $k$ trivial maps $\sph(x_j) \to *$. Integrating this fiberwise decomposition over the base space $\CP^{\times k}$, the pullback $R_k$ is similarly the colimit of the bloom of various maps of total spaces; but this bloom lives in a cube again seen (with a little care) to be equivalently the cube of coordinate planes in $\CP^{\times k}$. Consequently, $$ R_k \simeq W^k \CP .$$
nodes.statement_short: Name the pullback $R_k$, decompose its fibers as joins of circles, integrate the bloom over $\CP^{\times k}$, and recognize the coordinate-plane cube.

nodes.name: Name the pullback $R_k$
nodes.statement: To keep a handle on things, we'll start by naming the pullback itself $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \deloop U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ \CP^{\times k} \ar[r]_\oplus & \deloop U(k) }\end{xy} $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $R_k$ as the pullback of $\deloop U(k-1)\to\deloop U(k)\leftarrow \CP^{\times k}$.

nodes.name: Fibers of $R_k$ are joins of unpointed circles
nodes.statement: To begin with, note once more that a point of $R_k$ over $x : \CP^{\times k} $ is specified by a unit vector {\em in} $\oplus x$. Note furthermore that $x$ {\em is} (or might as well be) a {\em split} complex vector space: it comes with a prefered list of independent lines; this in turn gives the unit sphere in $\oplus x$, {\em canonically}, the structure of a join of (unpointed) circles: $$ \begin{xy}\xymatrix{ {\underset{j}{\bigstar}\,\sph(x_j)} \ar[r] \ar[d] & R_k \ar[r] \ar[d] & \deloop U(k-1) \ar[d] \\ {*} \ar[r]_{(x_j|j=1\dots k)} & \CP^{\times k} \ar[r] & \deloop U(k) }\end{xy}$$
nodes.statement_short: A point of $R_k$ is a unit vector in $\oplus x$; splitness of $x$ makes the unit sphere a join of circles.

nodes.name: The join is the colimit of the penultimate bloom
nodes.statement: Moreover, this join itself is the colimit of the penultimate bloom within the product cube of the $k$ trivial maps $\sph(x_j) \to *$.
nodes.statement_short: Recognize the join as a bloom colimit inside the product cube.

nodes.name: Integrate over $\CP^{\times k}$ and conclude $R_k \simeq W^k\CP$
nodes.statement: Integrating this fiberwise decomposition over the base space $\CP^{\times k}$, the pullback $R_k$ is similarly the colimit of the bloom of various maps of total spaces; but this bloom lives in a cube again seen (with a little care) to be equivalently the cube of coordinate planes in $\CP^{\times k}$. Consequently, $$ R_k \simeq W^k \CP .$$
nodes.statement_short: Globalize the fiberwise bloom to the coordinate-plane cube of $\CP^{\times k}$ and conclude.

nodes.name: The total cofiber $Y_k \simeq \deloop U(k)/P_k \simeq MU(k)/\Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k})$
nodes.statement: The cofiber --- let us call it $Y_k$ --- is, of course, the Total Cofiber of a pullback square, which means it is also the cofiber of the comparison map between the base $\deloop U(k)$ and the pushout of the pullback structure maps: $$\begin{xy}\xymatrix{ W^k\CP \bq k! \ar[r] \ar[d] & \deloop U(k-1) \ar[d] \ar@/^/[ddr] \\ \CP^{\times k} \bq k! \ar[r] \ar@/_/[drr] & P_k \ar[dr] \\ & & \deloop U(k) }\end{xy} $$ $$ Y_k \simeq \deloop U(k) / P_k \simeq MU(k) / \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k} ) $$
nodes.statement_short: $Y_k$, the cofiber of the comparison map, is the total cofiber of the pullback square, i.e. $\deloop U(k)/P_k$.

nodes.name: The group $G$: split extension $1\to\mathbb{T}^k\to G\to k!\to 1$
nodes.statement: As plainly as possible, there are a split extension of groups $$ 1\to \mathbb{T}^k \to G \to k!\to 1 $$ and various (conjugate) inclusions $$ \mathbb{T}^k \to G \to U(k) $$ realizing a maximal torus in $U(k)$. Concretely, one may take $G$ generated by the diagonal matrices and the permutation matrices.
nodes.statement_short: $G$ is the normalizer of the maximal torus in $U(k)$, generated by diagonal and permutation matrices.
differentia: one may take $G$ generated by the diagonal matrices and the permutation matrices

nodes.name: $\CP^{\times k}\bq k! \simeq \deloop G$ and $F_k \simeq U(k)\bq G$
nodes.statement: Continuing, $$ \CP^{\times k}\bq k! \simeq \deloop G $$ $$ F_k \simeq U(k) \bq G \simeq (U(k) \bq \mathbb{T}^k)\bq k! $$
nodes.statement_short: $\CP^{\times k}\bq k!$ classifies $G$; the fiber $F_k$ is the symmetrized flag manifold.

nodes.name: Disappointment: $\sph^{2k-1}\star F_k$ is not highly connected
nodes.statement: When I began working towards this note, I wanted to tell you how very-connected $\sph^{2k-1}\star F_k$ must be, but, alas, it is not!

nodes.name: Flag manifolds are simply connected, so $\pi_1 F_k \simeq k!$
nodes.statement: There is a simple induction argument that each (complex) flag manifold $V_k = U(k)\bq \mathbb{T}^k$ is simply connected: there are fiber sequences $$ V_k \to V_{k+1} \to \CP_k $$ and the base case $V_2 \simeq \CP_1$; this means that $\pi_1 F_k \simeq k!$, so that $\pi_2 \Sigma F_k \simeq C_2 = \mathrm{ab}(k!) $.
nodes.statement_short: Induction along $V_k\to V_{k+1}\to\CP_k$ gives $V_k$ simply connected, whence $\pi_1F_k\simeq k!$ and $\pi_2\Sigma F_k \simeq \mathrm{ab}(k!)$.
assumptions: there are fiber sequences $$ V_k \to V_{k+1} \to \CP_k $$
conclusions: each (complex) flag manifold $V_k = U(k)\bq \mathbb{T}^k$ is simply connected
$\pi_1 F_k \simeq k!$
$\pi_2 \Sigma F_k \simeq C_2 = \mathrm{ab}(k!) $

nodes.name: Rational cohomology of $L_{2k}$ is the $k!$-invariants
nodes.statement: Many readers, however, will already have concluded many things about the homology of the spaces $L_{2k}$. In particular, $$ H^*(L_{2k}; \QQ) \simeq (H^*(\CP^{\smsh k};\QQ))^{k!} $$ That is, the rational cohomology of $L_{2k}$ is the $k!$-invariants of the [already-torsion-free] homology of $\CP^{\smsh k}$ (because for finite $G$, all extensions of finitely-generated $\QQ[G]$-modules are split).
nodes.statement_short: $H^*(L_{2k};\QQ)$ is the ring of $k!$-invariants in $H^*(\CP^{\smsh k};\QQ)$, since $\QQ[G]$-modules split.

nodes.name: Borel-Serre: $H^*(\deloop U(k),\ZZ)$ is the $k!$-invariants of $H^*(\CP^{\times k};\ZZ)$
nodes.statement: A result that should be well-known due to Borel+Serre \cite{borSer} that in ordinary cohomology, $H^*(\deloop U(k),\ZZ) \to H^*(\CP^{\times k};\ZZ)$ is {\em exactly} the inclusion of the $k!$-invariants
nodes.statement_short: Borel-Serre: integral cohomology of $\deloop U(k)$ injects as exactly the symmetric-group invariants.
conclusions: in ordinary cohomology, $H^*(\deloop U(k),\ZZ) \to H^*(\CP^{\times k};\ZZ)$ is {\em exactly} the inclusion of the $k!$-invariants

nodes.name: $L_{2k} \to MU(k)$ is an equivalence modulo torsion
nodes.statement: it will follow from this, since we have an explicit-enough factorization of the maps $$ \CP^{\smsh k} \to \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) \to MU(k), $$ and from the multiplicative underpinning of the Thom isomorphism, that our map $L_{2k} \to MU(k)$ is an equivalence {\em modulo torsion}.
nodes.statement_short: Borel-Serre plus the Thom isomorphism make the comparison map $L_{2k}\to MU(k)$ an equivalence away from torsion.
assumptions: we have an explicit-enough factorization of the maps $$ \CP^{\smsh k} \to \Th(\deloop k!,\CP^{\smsh k}) \to MU(k), $$
the multiplicative underpinning of the Thom isomorphism
conclusions: our map $L_{2k} \to MU(k)$ is an equivalence {\em modulo torsion}

nodes.name: Complex cobordism is the initial torsion-free complex-orientable ring spectrum
nodes.statement: We can therefore, perhaps, give Ravenel the more concrete answer: Complex Cobordism is the initial {\em torsion-free} complex-orientable ring spectrum.
nodes.statement_short: The paper's tentative answer to Ravenel: $MU$ is initial among torsion-free complex-orientable ring spectra.
conclusions: Complex Cobordism is the initial {\em torsion-free} complex-orientable ring spectrum

nodes.name: Cartan-Leray spectral sequence for the Borel quotient
nodes.statement: The Cartan-Leray spectral sequence tells us $$ H_p( k! ; H_q(\CP^{\smsh k},\mathbb{F})) \Rightarrow H_{p+q} (\CP^{\smsh k}\bq k!) $$
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Group homology of $k!$ with coefficients in $H_*(\CP^{\smsh k})$ converges to the homology of the Borel quotient.
conclusions: $$ H_p( k! ; H_q(\CP^{\smsh k},\mathbb{F})) \Rightarrow H_{p+q} (\CP^{\smsh k}\bq k!) $$

nodes.name: Betley's homological stability lemma
nodes.statement: For any functor $T \in Ab^\Gamma$ of finite degree $d$, the natural map $$H_i( (n-1)! ; T ([n-1])) \to H_i( n! ; T([n])) $$ is an isomorphism provided $2i + d < n$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Twisted homology of symmetric groups with finite-degree coefficients stabilizes in the range $2i+d<n$.
nodes.origin_citation: Betley, Twisted homology of symmetric groups, Proc. AMS 130
assumptions: For any functor $T \in Ab^\Gamma$ of finite degree $d$
conclusions: the natural map $$H_i( (n-1)! ; T ([n-1])) \to H_i( n! ; T([n])) $$ is an isomorphism

nodes.name: Degree of an Abelian functor on $\Gamma$
nodes.statement: Here, $\Gamma$ is the category of {\em partial} maps of finite sets; the {\em degree} of such an Abelian functor is defined there in terms of the joint kernels of forgetting: a functor $T$ is of degree at-most $d$ whenever, for all $d$-part partitions $X = \coprod_j X_j$, the natural maps $$ T(X) \to \bigoplus_i T(\coprod_{j\neq i} X_j) $$ are all injective.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: $T$ has degree at most $d$ when the joint forgetting maps $T(X)\to\bigoplus_i T(\coprod_{j\neq i}X_j)$ are injective for all $d$-part partitions.
differentia: a functor $T$ is of degree at-most $d$ whenever, for all $d$-part partitions $X = \coprod_j X_j$, the natural maps $$ T(X) \to \bigoplus_i T(\coprod_{j\neq i} X_j) $$ are all injective

nodes.name: Cell-counting argument bounding the degree of $H_{2k+j}(\CP^{\smsh k})$
nodes.statement: For stable-homotopy purposes, we are interested in the homology groups $H_{2k+j}(\Th(k!,\CP^{\smsh k}))$ for $j\lesssim J$; that is, we are concerned only with the $2k+2J$-skeleton of the smash. Particularly, the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\CP^{\smsh k}$ consists of $\binom{J+k}{J}$ cells (apart from the basepoint). More: in $\CP^{\smsh k}$, nontrivial cells are products of $k$ nontrivial cells in $\CP$, of even dimensions, at least $2$; if their total dimension is not more than $2k+2J$, then at most $J$ of the factors are of dimension {\em greater} than $2$; that is, if $k > J$, all the cells in the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\CP^{\smsh k}$ are contained in an image of $$ \CP^{\smsh l} \smsh \sph^2 \smsh \CP^{\smsh k-l-1} \hookrightarrow \CP^{\smsh k} $$ and an easy amplification of this argument to $J+1$ smash factors leads us to the conclusion:
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Count cells of the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\CP^{\smsh k}$: at most $J$ factors exceed dimension $2$, so the functor has degree $\le J$.

nodes.name: Restrict attention to the $2k+2J$-skeleton
nodes.statement: For stable-homotopy purposes, we are interested in the homology groups $H_{2k+j}(\Th(k!,\CP^{\smsh k}))$ for $j\lesssim J$; that is, we are concerned only with the $2k+2J$-skeleton of the smash.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Set up: only the $2k+2J$-skeleton matters for the homology in the stable range.

nodes.name: At most $J$ smash factors exceed dimension $2$
nodes.statement: Particularly, the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\CP^{\smsh k}$ consists of $\binom{J+k}{J}$ cells (apart from the basepoint). More: in $\CP^{\smsh k}$, nontrivial cells are products of $k$ nontrivial cells in $\CP$, of even dimensions, at least $2$; if their total dimension is not more than $2k+2J$, then at most $J$ of the factors are of dimension {\em greater} than $2$; that is, if $k > J$, all the cells in the $2k+2J$-skeleton of $\CP^{\smsh k}$ are contained in an image of $$ \CP^{\smsh l} \smsh \sph^2 \smsh \CP^{\smsh k-l-1} \hookrightarrow \CP^{\smsh k} $$
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Bound the cells: every cell in the skeleton factors through $\CP^{\smsh l}\smsh\sph^2\smsh\CP^{\smsh k-l-1}$.

nodes.name: Amplify to $J+1$ smash factors
nodes.statement: and an easy amplification of this argument to $J+1$ smash factors leads us to the conclusion:
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by iterating the same argument with $J+1$ factors.

nodes.name: $H_{2k+j}(\CP^{\smsh k})$ extends as a functor of degree at most $J$
nodes.statement: $H_{2k+j}(\CP^{\smsh k})$, for $j < 2J$, extends along $[k] : \Gamma$ as a functor of degree at most $J$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: $H_{2k+j}(\CP^{\smsh k})$, for $j < 2J$, extends along $[k] : \Gamma$ as a functor of degree at most $J$.

nodes.name: Stabilization of $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\CP^{\smsh k}))$
nodes.statement: Consequently $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\CP^{\smsh k}))$ stabilizes for $2 p + J \leq k$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
conclusions: $H_p(k!;H_{2k+j}(\CP^{\smsh k}))$ stabilizes for $2 p + J \leq k$

nodes.name: Stability of the Cartan-Leray $E^2$ pages and of the $L_{2k}$
nodes.statement: This establishes that the pages $E^2_{*,*}$ of the Cartan-Leray spectral sequences are stable in the sense necessary for $L_{2k}$ to approximate a finite-type spectrum; concluding that $L_{2k}$ themselves stabilize reduces to arguing that the prespectrum maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to \CP\smsh L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ {\em realize} the morphisms shown in \mbox{Lemma \ref{betstable}} to become isomorphisms; but this already follows from the usual calculation of $H_i(\CP^{\smsh k})$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Stable $E^2$ pages give finite type; identifying the prespectrum maps with Betley's stabilization morphisms finishes it.

nodes.name: The $E^2$ pages are stable in the required sense
nodes.statement: This establishes that the pages $E^2_{*,*}$ of the Cartan-Leray spectral sequences are stable in the sense necessary for $L_{2k}$ to approximate a finite-type spectrum
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Combine the above: the Cartan-Leray $E^2$ pages stabilize, so a finite-type spectrum is approximated.

nodes.name: Prespectrum maps realize Betley's stabilization morphisms
nodes.statement: concluding that $L_{2k}$ themselves stabilize reduces to arguing that the prespectrum maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to \CP\smsh L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ {\em realize} the morphisms shown in \mbox{Lemma \ref{betstable}} to become isomorphisms; but this already follows from the usual calculation of $H_i(\CP^{\smsh k})$.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Apply Betley's lemma: the prespectrum maps induce exactly the stabilization isomorphisms, by the known $H_i(\CP^{\smsh k})$.

nodes.name: The $L_{2k}$ approximate the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum
nodes.statement: The spaces $L_{2k}$ with the maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$ approximate a finite-type commutative ring spectrum $\Lambda$; this is the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum.
nodes.section: 9 Stabilization; or, $L_*$ presents a finite-type spectrum
nodes.statement_short: $\{L_{2k}\}$ presents a finite-type commutative ring spectrum $\Lambda$, initial among complex-oriented ones.
assumptions: The spaces $L_{2k}$ with the maps $\Sigma^2 L_{2k} \to L_{2(k+1)}$
conclusions: approximate a finite-type commutative ring spectrum $\Lambda$
this is the initial complex-oriented commutative ring spectrum
